result:
A race condition is when two processes touch shared state at the same time and the result depends on which one happens to run first. With a shared log, two scripts writing at once can interleave their output mid-line or, if either one truncates or rewrites the file, lose entries.

Take an exclusive lock around the write with `flock`, and always append with `>>`:

```sh
{
  flock -x 9
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg" >&9
} 9>>/var/log/shared.log
```

The lock is released when the block ends and fd 9 closes, even if the script dies. Every writer must use the same lock for it to work, since `flock` is advisory and a process that skips it is not blocked. It is unreliable on NFS; there, give each process its own log file instead.

Never read-modify-write the log (for example `sed -i`, or `cat log > tmp; mv tmp log`) without holding the same lock, because that is where entries get lost.
